title: Fort Garland Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Fort Garland wells have a 130-foot median depth; see local yields, water levels, permit history, and drilling costs.
h1: Fort Garland, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Fort Garland means evaluating the well record, not just the view or the asking price. Permitted wells within five miles show a broad range of depths, but most are completed in the local unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. The records also show useful differences between drilling depth, reported yield, and the depth to standing water.

This page uses Colorado Division of Water Resources permit data to give you a practical starting point for a land purchase, replacement well, or new build near Fort Garland. A nearby permit is evidence, not a guarantee. The exact lot, aquifer conditions, access, and intended use still control the final result.

sections.heading: Fort Garland well depths reflect mixed ground conditions
sections.html:
The median permitted well near Fort Garland is 130 feet deep. The middle half runs from 60 to 225 feet, so a driller bidding a typical residential well should not assume that every hole will resemble the median. About 36% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 51% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

The deeper tail matters for budgeting. About 12% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 1% reach beyond 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 982 feet. Local ground is described as mixed sedimentary and alluvial material, with many permits naming an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Fractured ground can make the exact depth less predictable from one parcel to the next.

sections.heading: Expected well yield around Fort Garland
sections.html:
Among wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 11.1 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. That is a useful working range for a household well, but it is not a promise for an untested property. Only 152 wells report a pump yield, so the yield data is a subset of the permit record.

The distribution is generally favorable: 59% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 36% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 5% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while none of the reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for a pump test and learn the permitted use before relying on a neighboring well's output.

sections.heading: Water levels and what the Fort Garland record shows
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth from the ground surface down to standing water when the well is not being pumped. The local median is 50 feet, with the middle half between 30 and 96 feet. That information can help a contractor think about pump setting, trench work, and how much lift the system may need, but it does not replace a site-specific measurement.

The decade comparison does not show a simple dropping water table. The median measured level was 80 feet below surface in the 2010s and 45 feet below surface in the 2020s, meaning the later reported water was shallower. Measurements can come from different wells, locations, seasons, and conditions, so treat this as a record-level indication rather than a basin-wide conclusion.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers serving the area
sections.html:
Fort Garland has a long permit record, with 740 wells in the Colorado DWR data and 533 recorded as constructed. Permits were issued in every listed decade, including 153 in the 2010s and 125 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. The use mix is mainly domestic or household at 55%, followed by monitoring at 22%, irrigation at 15%, and stock use at 9%.

The most active drillers in these records are Heersink Drilling with 71 permits, Mitchell Drilling Co. with 46, and Valley Pump Company with 21. These names show permit activity, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, availability, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new Fort Garland well may cost
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground reported around Fort Garland, the drilling rate model is $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 130 feet, that puts the drilled hole at about $6,500 to $9,800. This is the hole itself, not the complete water system.

A finished installation with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $12,500 to $21,800. A bid can move outside that range if the hole is deeper than expected, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the lot needs unusual trenching and power work. Get the contractor to separate drilling, casing, testing, pump equipment, electrical, and site restoration so you can compare bids accurately.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying near Fort Garland
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported data, but a record without a yield is not proof of a productive well. Of the 740 permits, only 152 report pump yield, and 538 report a total depth. A dry hole or weak fracture can still occur on a parcel that has a good well nearby. Check the well construction report, pump test, water level, casing, grout, and current equipment condition.

There are 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 historic mine features mapped within about ten miles. No EPA Superfund or cleanup sites are mapped in that area. That does not make private water automatically safe. Test the proposed well for relevant contaminants, inspect nearby land uses, and keep septic setbacks, replacement-area needs, building placement, and access for drilling equipment in the site plan.

sections.heading: A practical lot review for Fort Garland buyers
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare permits nearby in Fort Garland, Blanca, and the surrounding Costilla County area. Neighboring wells can help establish a realistic depth and yield range, but they are not a guarantee in fractured-bedrock ground. Confirm the permit's authorized use: domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells do not all support the same plans.

Before closing, have a Colorado well contractor review access for a rig, likely drilling depth, pump location, storage, electrical service, and septic layout. If you plan a home, confirm the well permit and any augmentation-plan requirements with the state and local authorities. For an existing well, obtain a current flow test and laboratory water test rather than relying on an old seller statement.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Fort Garland?
faq.a: The median permitted well near Fort Garland is 130 feet deep. The middle half runs from 60 to 225 feet, while 51% are between 100 and 300 feet. Some wells are much deeper: 12% fall between 300 and 600 feet, 1% exceed 600 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 982 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Fort Garland?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 130-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,500 to $9,800. A finished system including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,500 to $21,800. Actual bids depend on depth, access, construction, and site work.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Fort Garland?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 11.1 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 59% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 36% report more than 15. Only 152 wells report yield, so a pump test remains important for a specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Fort Garland?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that private well water is safe to drink. Within about ten miles, the mapped record includes 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 historic mine features. No EPA Superfund or cleanup sites are mapped. Test the actual well for bacteria, minerals, and site-relevant contaminants before drinking it.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well in Fort Garland?
faq.a: Review the DWR permit, construction report, authorized use, pump test, static water level, casing, grout, and recent water test. The area has 740 permitted wells, but only 533 are recorded as constructed and 152 report pump yield. Also verify rig access, septic placement, electrical needs, and any augmentation-plan requirements for your intended use.
